KEY MESSAGE 1...

High pressure is near southeast New England this morning with a
stationary front over the eastern Great Lakes Region, western NY
and and w-central PA. The mid and upper-level flow will be west
to northwest with ridging over the Upper Midwest, northern 
Great Lakes Region and Ontario. A mid and upper level short-wave
and the frontal boundary lifting slightly north and east in the
mid to late morning will focus showers with some embedded 
thunderstorms. Mean MUCAPE values on the latest HREF are 
generally under 300 J/kg with negative Showalter stability 
indices indicative of some elevated instability today. The low 
pressure system or weakening MCS on some of the CAMS is 
supported by the right entrance region of a mid and upper level 
jet streak which will enhanced the lift and pcpn. PWATs will be 
in the 1.50-2.0" range from north to south across the region 
which are 1-2.5" STDEVS above normal according to HREFs. 

Based on several of the CAMs, the heaviest rainfall looks like 
it will fall from the Mohawk Valley, Greater Capital Region and 
the Berkshires northward. Hourly rainfall rates based on the 
latest HREF could briefly be in the 0.25-0.50" range with some 
locally higher amounts up to an inch/hr. The rainfall should 
diminish by the late morning/early evening with an outflow 
boundary drifting southward which may focus a severe threat for
the later afternoon. An isolated flash flood (WPC Day 1 ERO
Level 1 of 4) threat exists with any enhanced rainfall rates, 
though gridded 1-hr/3-hr FFG values remain high. At the very 
least, ponding of water on roadways/low-lying areas for the
morning commute and/or poor drainage flooding of urban areas 
will be possible. Plenty of clouds and spotty light rain will 
linger into the afternoon, especially north of the mid Hudson 
Valley and eastern Catskills.  

KEY MESSAGE 2...

The warm front stalls and actually retreats back to the
south/southwest in the late afternoon/evening. It is possible 
on the warm side of the boundary that some strong to potentially
severe thunderstorms develop. The focus will be an outflow 
boundary from the morning system and the front. The latest 
HREFs still show mean SBCAPEs of 750-1500 J/kg with 0-6 km deep 
shear 40-45 KT along the west/southwest border of the WFO ALY 
forecast area across the northern/eastern Catskills, mid Hudson 
Valley, southern Taconics and NW CT. SPC maintains a Marginal 
Risk (Level 1 of 5) for most this region with a Slight Risk 
(Level 2 of 5) for Ulster and Dutchess Counties close to I-84. A
gradient of instability exists and overlaps with shear with a 
potential outflow boundary. Some of the CAMs show the potential 
for some organized deep convection with an isolated super cell 
threat with damaging winds and large hail the main hazards. 
However, with a boundary and some backed low-level flow with 
enhanced 0-1 km helicity/shear and potential low LCL heights, 
an isolated tornado can not be ruled out in the mid Hudson 
Valley or close to the I-84 corridor. If it remains cloudy, then
severe/strong thunderstorm threat will diminish late this pm 
and into tonight. Max temps will run cool from the I-90 corridor
north and east with the east to northeast low-level flow and we
blended with MAV MOS with the NBM for highs in the mid 60s to 
lower 70s in these areas with some mid 70s to around 80F 
southward. 

KEY MESSAGE 3...

Much of Tue night into early Wed will be mostly cloudy with some
patchy light rain showers/drizzle with patchy fog due to the
1025 hPa or sfc high keeping the frontal boundary south and west
of the region. However, a strong mid/upper level short-wave and
an occluded front approaches from the west Wed pm. The timing
for any strong to severe thunderstorms looks to be in the late
pm into the early evening. On some of the CAMs, an MCS forms
over southeast Ontario and the eastern Great Lakes in the mid to
late pm and races towards the western Dacks/western Mohawk.
MUCAPES rise to 1000-1500 J/kg west of the Hudson River Valley 
with MLCAPES in 750 J/kg or less. The deep shear remains 40-50 
KT. SPC introduced in the latest Day 2 Outlook a Marginal Risk 
(Level 1 of 5) for locations west and southwest of Albany. 
Isolated instances of damaging winds and large hail would be the
main threats. The limited instability along and east of the 
Hudson River Valley should limit the severe threat. 

The heavy rainfall threat still exists Wed night into Thu
morning, PWATs remain 1 to 2 STDEVS above normal in the 1.5-2.0"
range on the various CAMs. The strongly forced wave could
produce some training/back building convection especially from
the Schoharie Valley and the Capital Region north and west.
Hourly rainfall rates 1" or more an hour could occur. WPC
maintains a Slight Risk (Level 2 of 4) for scattered instances
of flash flooding possible from the Schoharie Valley/Capital
